method: I chose one template and wrote my Access Rider by filling in it. I put in my own needs for workspace, communication, rest, and travel. Otherwise, I tried to keep it simple and clear so others can understand it easily. I left out some private details like emergency contact.
related_work: I used the templates from our tutor. I also looked at the Criptech article by Chang and Felt to think about access as more than just a list of things I need.
references:
[1] Class template for Access Rider.
[2] Johanna Hedva, “Disability Access Rider,” 2022.
[3] Chang and Felt, “Criptech and the Art of Access,” Leonardo, 2024
results_discussion: My Access Rider has sections for permissions, access requirements, mental health, communication, and hours. It shows that access is about how people talk and work together. I learned that writing things down helps me feel more in control. One hard part was deciding what to share because some needs feel personal. I also saw that the form itself can be a way to ask for change, not just a list of complaints.
title: W1
introduction: This week I learned how to write an Access Rider. By writing one myself  rider, I will answer the question “How do I make an Access Rider if I am disabled?” . I want to see how it can help me explain my needs at work.
